nodes.name: p-variate Gaussian random field on a metric graph
nodes.statement: The purpose of the work is to construct a $p$-variate Gaussian {random field}, denoted $\rVec{Z}:= \{ \rVec{Z}(u)=(Z_1(u),\ldots,Z_p(u))^{\top}, \; u \in {\cal G} \}$ throughout and defined over a metric graph, $\mathcal G$, with a given matrix-valued covariance function that is isotropic, that is it depends on the {\em distance} between the points of the graph.

nodes.name: Graph with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement: The type of topology considered by \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020} (to which the reader is referred for additional details and motivation) is called graph {\em with Euclidean edges}, denoted with a triple ${\cal G}=\left( V,E,\{\varphi_e\}_{e\in E} \right)$ throughout, where the elements are blended in the following way: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] {{$(V, E)$}} has a graph structure, \textit{i.e. } $V$ is the set of vertices and {$E\subset V\times V$} accounts for the edges. We assume that this graph is simple and connected, \textit{i.e. } $V$ is finite, the graph has not repeated edges or edges that join a vertex to itself and every pair of vertices is connected by a path. \item[(b)] Each edge $e\in E$ is provided with a \emph{length} $\ell(e)>0$ and a \emph{weight} $w(e):=1/\ell(e)$; furthermore, it is associated with a unique abstract set, also denoted $e$, such that $V$ and all the edge sets are mutually disjoint. \item[(c)] Let $v_1$ and $v_2$ be vertices connected by $e\in E$. Then, $\varphi_e$ is a continuous and bijective mapping defined on $e \cup \{v_1,v_2\}$, such that $\varphi_e$ maps $e$ onto an open interval $(0,\ell(e)) \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $\{v_1,v_2\}$ onto $\{0,\ell(e)\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement_short: A simple connected graph whose edges carry lengths and are bijectively mapped to real intervals (0, l(e)).
nodes.label: def:graphWithEE

nodes.name: Total order on vertices and edge orientation
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we shall assume the existence of a total order relation on the set of vertices $V$ and that every edge is represented through the ordered pair $(v_1,v_2)$, where $v_1<v_2$.

nodes.name: Point representation u = (u_lower, u_upper, delta)
nodes.statement: {By abuse of notation, we write} {$u\in\mathcal G$ to denote a point on the graph: it can be either a vertex or a point on an edge. Each point $u\in \mathcal G$ will be identified with the triple $(\ul u, \ol u, \delta)$, where: $\ul u < \ol u$ are the endpoints of the edge $e$ containing $u$ and $\delta \in [0,1]$ is the relative distance of $u$ from $\ul u$; formally: $\delta=\delta(u):=w(e)\varphi_e(u)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Gaussian {random fields} on graphs with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement_short: A point u of G is identified by its edge endpoints and its relative position delta(u) in [0,1] along the edge.

nodes.name: Edge map e(u)
nodes.statement: Finally, we use the notation $e(u)$, where $e:\mathcal G \to E$, to denote the edge that contains $u$. If $u\in V$, then $e(u)$ is any of the edges that have an endpoint in $u$.

nodes.statement: A graph with Euclidean edges is called an \emph{Euclidean tree} if it has a tree structure, \textit{i.e. } given any two points $u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal{G}$, there is exactly one path that connects $u_1$ to $u_2$.

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite and conditionally negative semidefinite matrices
nodes.statement: An $n\times n$ real matrix $\latMatr A$ is said to be \emph{positive semidefinite} if and only if $\dVec{c}^\top \latMatr{A} \dVec{c} \geq 0$ for all $\dVec{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and \emph{conditionally negative semidefinite} if and only if $\dVec{c}^\top \latMatr{A} \dVec{c} \leq 0$ for all $\dVec{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top \dVec{c} = 0$.

nodes.name: Quasi-Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: An $n\times n$ matrix $\latMatr L$ is called \emph{quasi-Laplacian} if and only if it is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and has exactly one null eigenvalue, with corresponding eigenvector ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$.

nodes.name: Laplacian matrix of a graph with Euclidean edges
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we will consider the Laplacian matrix of a given graph with Euclidean edges, with entries defined as \citet[Equation (1)]{devriendt_effective_2022}: {\begin{equation} L_{ij} = \begin{dcases} \sum_{v\in V} w((v, v_i)) &\text{ if $i=j$}\\ -w((v_i,v_j)) &\text{ if $i \neq j$,} \end{dcases} \end{equation} with $w((v_i,v_j))$ the weight of the edge joining vertices $v_i$ and $v_j$ if these vertices are connected, $0$ otherwise.}

Then the following statements hold. \begin{enumerate} \item ${\latMatr{B}}\ne \grMatr 0$. \item ${\latMatr{A}}$ and ${\latMatr{C}}$ are strictly positive definite. \item Both ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}:={\latMatr{A}}-{\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}^\top$ and ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{A}}:={\latMatr{C}} - {\latMatr{B}}^\top {\latMatr{A}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}$ are quasi-Laplacian matrices, \textit{i.e. }, the set of quasi-Laplacian matrices is closed under the Schur complement operation. \item ${\latMatr{L}}^-$ is a quasi-Laplacian matrix. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Variogram
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set and $Z:X\to \mathbb{R}$ a square-integrable random {field}. The \emph{variogram} of $Z$ is defined via \begin{align} \gamma_{{Z}}: X\times X &\to \mathbb{R} \nonumber\\ (x_1,x_2)&\mapsto \gamma_{{Z}} (x_1,x_2):=\mathbb{V}ar\round{{Z}(x_1)-{Z}(x_2)}.\nonumber \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The variogram of Z is gamma(x1,x2)=Var(Z(x1)-Z(x2)).

nodes.name: Variogram is conditionally negative semidefinite
nodes.statement: Clearly, a variogram is always symmetric and non-negative valued. In addition, it is conditionally negative semidefinite, \textit{i.e. } it satisfies \citep{chiles2012geostatistics} \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j \gamma(x_i,x_j) \leq 0 \end{equation} whenever $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i = 0$, for any $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$.
assumptions: whenever $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i = 0$, for any $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$
conclusions: a variogram is always symmetric and non-negative valued

nodes.name: Conditional negative semidefiniteness of variograms
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j \gamma(x_i,x_j) \leq 0

nodes.name: Resistance metric
nodes.statement: \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020} define the resistance metric, denoting $d_R$ throughout, as the variogram of a {random field} $Z$ on the graph with Euclidean edges $\mathcal G$, that is constructed {\em ad hoc} in order to be as much as possibly parenthetical to a Brownian bridge on the graph.
nodes.statement_short: d_R is the variogram of an ad hoc Brownian-bridge-like random field on the graph with Euclidean edges.

nodes.name: Pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: The concept of variogram can be generalised to the case of a zero-mean square-integrable vector-valued random field $\rVec{Z}$ on a non-empty set $X$, through the following lines. The \emph{pseudo-variogram} of $\rVec{Z}$ is defined through the identity \begin{align} \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}:X\times X &\to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}\nonumber \\ (x_1,x_2) &\mapsto \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(x_1,x_2):=\Big [ \mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(x_1)-Z_j(x_2)} \Big ]_{i,j=1}^p. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The pseudo-variogram of a vector field Z is the matrix [Var(Z_i(x1)-Z_j(x2))]_{ij}.

nodes.name: Pseudo-variogram definition
nodes.statement: \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}:X\times X &\to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}\nonumber \\ (x_1,x_2) &\mapsto \grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(x_1,x_2):=\Big [ \mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(x_1)-Z_j(x_2)} \Big ]_{i,j=1}^p.
nodes.label: eq:pseudoVariogramDef

nodes.name: Matrix form of the pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: Straightforward calculations allow to rewrite the above as \begin{equation} \grMatr \Gamma_{\boldsymbol{Z}}(x_1,x_2) = \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)} \,{\mathbf{1}_{p}}^\top + {\mathbf{1}_{p}}\, \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}^\top - 2\, \Cov{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)}{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}, \end{equation} where $\mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ is the $p\times p$ {collocated} variance-covariance matrix of $\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$, $\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ is the $p\times 1$ vector containing the main diagonal of $\mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ and $\Cov{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)}{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}:=\Exp{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)^\top}$.
assumptions: where $\mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$ is the $p\times p$ {collocated} variance-covariance matrix of $\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)$
conclusions: Straightforward calculations allow to rewrite the above as
nodes.statement_short: Pseudo-variogram = diag variances of each point spread over rows/columns minus twice the cross-covariance.

nodes.statement: \grMatr \Gamma_{\boldsymbol{Z}}(x_1,x_2) = \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)} \,{\mathbf{1}_{p}}^\top + {\mathbf{1}_{p}}\, \round{\mathrm{diag} \mathbb{V}ar \boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)}^\top - 2\, \Cov{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_1)}{\boldsymbol{Z}(x_2)},

nodes.name: Properties of the pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: The pseudo-variogram satisfies the following properties \citep{dorr2023characterization}: \begin{itemize} \item {for any $x_1,x_2 \in X$,} \begin{equation} \grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_1,x_2)=\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_2,x_1)^\top; \end{equation} \item {for any $x \in X$, the diagonal entries of $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x,x)$ are zero;} \item $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}$ is ${\mathbf{1}_{p}}$-conditionally negative semidefinite, \textit{i.e. } for all {$n \in \mathbb{N}^+$, $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$ and } $\dVec c_1,\dots,\dVec c_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$ such that $ {{\mathbf{1}_{p}}}^\top \sum_{i=1}^n \dVec c_i = 0$, it holds \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec c_i^\top \grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_i,x_j) \dVec c_j \leq 0. \end{equation} \end{itemize}
conclusions: for any $x \in X$, the diagonal entries of $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x,x)$ are zero;
nodes.statement_short: A pseudo-variogram is transpose-symmetric, has zero diagonal at coincident points, and is 1_p-conditionally negative semidefinite.

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite function
nodes.statement: A function $k:X\times X \to \mathbb{R}$ is positive semidefinite if, for all $n\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$, ${x}_1,\dots,{x}_n \in X$ and $c_1,\dots,c_n \in \mathbb{R}$, one has \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j k({x}_i, {x}_j) \geq 0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite matrix-valued function
nodes.statement: A matrix-valued function $\latMatr K :X\times X \to \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is positive semidefinite if, for all $n\in\curly{1,2,\dots}$, ${\dVec{c}}_1,\dots,{\dVec{c}}_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$ and ${x}_1,\dots,{x}_n\in X$, it holds: \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n {\dVec{c}}_i^\top \latMatr{K}(x_i,x_j) {\dVec{c}}_j \geq 0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Strictly positive definite matrix-valued function
nodes.statement: In addition, $\latMatr{K}$ is strictly positive definite if it is positive semidefinite and the condition \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n {\dVec{c}}_i^\top \latMatr K ({x}_i,{x}_j) {\dVec{c}}_j = 0 \end{equation} implies that there exists a pair $ i\ne j$ such that ${x}_i={x}_j$ or ${\dVec{c}}_1=\dots={\dVec{c}}_n=0$.

nodes.name: Completely monotone function
nodes.statement: A function $\psi:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ is called \emph{completely monotone} if it is continuous on $[0,+\infty)$, infinitely differentiable on $(0,+\infty)$ and for each $i\in \mathbb{N}$ it holds \begin{equation*} (-1)^i\,\psi^{(i)}(x)\geq 0, \end{equation*} where $\psi^{(i)}$ denotes the $i^\text{th}$ derivative of $\psi$ and $\psi^{(0)}:=\psi$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations

nodes.name: Bernstein's characterisation of completely monotone functions
nodes.statement: A function $\psi:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ is completely monotone if and only if it is the Laplace transform of a (unique) finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $[0,+\infty)$, \textit{i.e. } \begin{equation} \psi(x)=\int_0^{+\infty} \exp(-tx) \, \mu({\rm d}t), \quad x\in [0,+\infty). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.5 Classes of functions and Schoenberg characterisations
conclusions: is completely monotone if and only if it is the Laplace transform of a (unique) finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $[0,+\infty)$
equivalent_conditions: it is the Laplace transform of a (unique) finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $[0,+\infty)$

nodes.name: Laplace transform representation
nodes.statement: \psi(x)=\int_0^{+\infty} \exp(-tx) \, \mu({\rm d}t), \quad x\in [0,+\infty).

nodes.name: Bernstein function
nodes.statement: A function $g:[0,+\infty) \to [0,+\infty)$ is called a \emph{Bernstein function} if $g$ in infinitely differentiable on $[0,+\infty)$ and $g^{(1)}$ is a completely monotone function.

nodes.name: Multivariate Schoenberg theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\psi: [0,+\infty)\to {(0,+\infty)}$ be a {non-constant} completely monotone function, $g:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ {be} a Bernstein function and let $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}: X\times X\to [0,+\infty)^{p\times p}$, for a non-empty set $X$. If, for all ${x_1,x_2}\in X$, $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}^\top(x_1,x_2)=\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_2,x_1)$ and $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}$ is ${\mathbf{1}_{p}}$-conditionally negative semidefinite, then, for all ${\xi}>0$, \begin{equation*} ({x_1,x_2})\mapsto \psi\Big ({\xi} \, g\round{\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}({x_1,x_2}}\Big ), \qquad {x_1,x_2}\in X, \end{equation*} where $\psi$ and $g$ are applied element-wise, is a positive semidefinite function on $X$.

assumptions: Let $\psi: [0,+\infty)\to {(0,+\infty)}$ be a {non-constant} completely monotone function
$g:[0,+\infty)\to {[0,+\infty)}$ {be} a Bernstein function
for all ${x_1,x_2}\in X$, $\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}^\top(x_1,x_2)=\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}(x_2,x_1)$
$\grMatr \Gamma_{{\rVec{Z}}}$ is ${\mathbf{1}_{p}}$-conditionally negative semidefinite
conclusions: is a positive semidefinite function on $X$.
nodes.statement_short: psi(xi g(Gamma)) applied element-wise is positive semidefinite for completely monotone psi, Bernstein g and a 1_p-CNSD transpose-symmetric Gamma.
nodes.label: theo:MultivariateSchoenberg

nodes.name: Notation n, L, Sigma, Lambda, W and M_p
nodes.statement: The following notation will ease the exposition throughout: \begin{itemize} \item $n$ is the number of vertices of {the graph} ${\cal G}$ (cardinality of $V$), \item ${\latMatr{L}}$ is the Laplacian matrix of ${\cal G}$ as per Equation (\ref{eq:laplacianofagraph}), \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}:={\latMatr{L}}^-$ is the Moore-Penrose inverse of ${\latMatr{L}}$, \item ${\grMatr{\Lambda}}$ and ${\latMatr{W}}$ are the eigenvalues and eigenvectors matrices of ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}$, \textit{i.e. } ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = {\latMatr{W}} {\grMatr{\Lambda}} {\latMatr{W}}^\top$, \item for two matrices ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}$ {of the same size} and for a positive integer $p$, we define \begin{equation} \Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:={\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - {\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{A}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{A}} \end{bmatrix}. \end{equation} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: n vertices, Laplacian L, Sigma = L^- with eigendecomposition W Lambda W^T, and the block matrix M_p(A,B) with A on the diagonal and B off it.

nodes.name: Block matrix M_p(A,B)
nodes.statement: \Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}:={\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - {\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{A}} & \dots & {\latMatr{B}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ {\latMatr{B}} & {\latMatr{B}} & \dots & {\latMatr{A}} \end{bmatrix}.
nodes.label: eq:notationM

nodes.name: Additive construction Z = Z_V + Z_E
nodes.statement: Specifically, we shall consider a vector-valued random field, $\rVec{Z}$, that is obtained through the identity \begin{equation} \rVec{Z}(u) := \rVec{Z}_{V}(u) + \rVec{Z}_{E}(u), \qquad u \in \mathcal G. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Random field as sum of vertex and edge fields
nodes.statement: \rVec{Z}(u) := \rVec{Z}_{V}(u) + \rVec{Z}_{E}(u), \qquad u \in \mathcal G.
nodes.label: eq:multivariate_random_field_Z

nodes.name: Desideratum D1: diagonal variograms as in Anderes et al.
nodes.statement: The construction (\ref{eq:multivariate_random_field_Z}) needs to provide a pseudo-variogram $\grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}$ for which the diagonal entries should obey to the variogram construction as in \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}.

nodes.name: Desideratum D2: block-precision matrix Theta
nodes.statement: The multivariate {random field} $\rVec{Z}_V$ on $V$ should enjoy a homogeneous conditional independence structure. More precisely, we set the block-precision matrix ${\grMatr{\Theta}}$ of $\rVec{Z}_V$ to have the following structure: \begin{equation} {\grMatr{\Theta}} = \Mv{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha {\latMatr{I}_n}}, \end{equation} where $\alpha$ is a positive real value and $\latMatr{Q}$ is a suitable $n\times n$ matrix that will be defined next. This means that, for $i\ne j$ and $v_1\ne v_2$, ${Z}_{V,i}(v_1)$ and $Z_{V,j}(v_2)$ are conditionally independent given everything else.
nodes.statement_short: Z_V on V has homogeneous conditional independence: its block precision is Theta = M_p(Q, -alpha I_n).

nodes.name: Block-precision matrix Theta
nodes.statement: {\grMatr{\Theta}} = \Mv{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha {\latMatr{I}_n}},
nodes.label: eq:defTheta

nodes.name: Matrices Q and X
nodes.statement: Define the $n\times n$ matrices: \begin{align} \latMatr{Q}&:=\frac{1}{2} \round{{\latMatr{L}}+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{\latMatr{L}^2-2\alpha (p-2){\latMatr{L}}+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2} {\latMatr{W}} \round{{\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{({\grMatr{\Lambda}}^{-})^2-2\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}} {\latMatr{W}}^\top,\\ {\latMatr{X}}&:=\frac{1}{\alpha(p-1)}\round{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr{Q} - {\latMatr{I}_n}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2\alpha (p-1)} {\latMatr{W}} \round{\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \sqrt{{\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n} - 2 \alpha (p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \alpha^2 p^2 {\grMatr{\Lambda}}^2} -{\latMatr{I}_n}-\latMatr{J}_n} {\latMatr{W}}^\top. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Q is a square-root expression in L, alpha and p; X = (Sigma Q - I)/(alpha(p-1)); both also given via the eigendecomposition of Sigma.

nodes.name: Definition of Q
nodes.statement: \latMatr{Q}&:=\frac{1}{2} \round{{\latMatr{L}}+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{\latMatr{L}^2-2\alpha (p-2){\latMatr{L}}+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2} {\latMatr{W}} \round{{\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha(p-2){\latMatr{I}_n}+\sqrt{({\grMatr{\Lambda}}^{-})^2-2\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}}^-+\alpha^2 p^2 {\latMatr{I}_n}}} {\latMatr{W}}^\top,
nodes.label: eq:defQ

nodes.name: Definition of X
nodes.statement: {\latMatr{X}}&:=\frac{1}{\alpha(p-1)}\round{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr{Q} - {\latMatr{I}_n}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2\alpha (p-1)} {\latMatr{W}} \round{\alpha(p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \sqrt{{\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n} - 2 \alpha (p-2){\grMatr{\Lambda}} + \alpha^2 p^2 {\grMatr{\Lambda}}^2} -{\latMatr{I}_n}-\latMatr{J}_n} {\latMatr{W}}^\top.
nodes.label: eq:defX

nodes.name: Spectral forms of Q and X
nodes.statement: Notice that in Equations (\ref{eq:defQEigen}) and (\ref{eq:defXEigen}) the principal square root coincides with the element-wise square root, being its arguments diagonal matrices. {These equations have been established from Equations (\ref{eq:defQ}) and (\ref{eq:defX}) by using the fact that $\latMatr{W}$ is an orthogonal matrix and that $\grMatr{\Lambda} \grMatr{\Lambda}^- = \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n$ insofar as the first $p-1$ diagonal entries of $\grMatr{\Lambda}$ are positive and the last diagonal entry is zero.}

nodes.name: Constants k_1, k_2 and matrices Sigma-tilde, X-tilde
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the two positive constants \begin{equation*} k_1 := \frac{p-1}{\alpha n p^2} \qquad k_2 := \frac{p^2-p+1}{\alpha n p^2(p-1)}, \end{equation*} and the $n \times n$ matrices \begin{equation*} \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} := {\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} \qquad \Tilde {\latMatr{X}} := {\latMatr{X}} + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the construction under the desiderata
nodes.statement: Although these definitions may appear {peculiar}, they are the only solution to the \emph{desiderata} $\mathbb D$ previously stated and are crucial to define the random field $\rVec{Z}_V$.
conclusions: they are the only solution to the \emph{desiderata} $\mathbb D$ previously stated

nodes.name: Covariance of Z_V on the vertices
nodes.statement: We start with the vertices, where $\rVec{Z}_V$ is assumed a zero-mean $p$-variate Gaussian random vector $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V:V\to \mathbb{R}^p$ having covariance matrix-valued function \begin{equation} \Cov{\rVec{Z}_V(v_1)}{\rVec{Z}_V(v_2)}:=\Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}[v_1, v_2]}{\Tilde {\latMatr{X}}[v_1, v_2]} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On vertices Z_V is a zero-mean Gaussian vector with covariance M_p(Sigma~[v1,v2], X~[v1,v2]).

nodes.name: Vertex covariance of Z_V
nodes.statement: \Cov{\rVec{Z}_V(v_1)}{\rVec{Z}_V(v_2)}:=\Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}[v_1, v_2]}{\Tilde {\latMatr{X}}[v_1, v_2]} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}.
nodes.label: eq:covZ_V_onV

nodes.name: Theta and its Moore-Penrose inverse are quasi-Laplacian
nodes.statement: The matrix $\grMatr \Theta$ defined in Equation (\ref{eq:defTheta}) and its Moore-Penrose inverse $\grMatr \Theta^-$ are quasi-Laplacian.
conclusions: The matrix $\grMatr \Theta$ defined in Equation (\ref{eq:defTheta}) and its Moore-Penrose inverse $\grMatr \Theta^-$ are quasi-Laplacian.
nodes.label: prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian

nodes.name: Vertex covariance is positive semidefinite
nodes.statement: The function defined in (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) is positive semidefinite.
conclusions: The function defined in (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) is positive semidefinite.
nodes.label: prop:covZ_V_isACov

nodes.name: Linear interpolation of Z_V on edges
nodes.statement: Once $\rVec{Z}_V$ is defined over the vertices, the corresponding values over the edges are attained through a sheer linear interpolation. Namely, for $u=(\ul u, \ol u,\delta(u))\in \mathcal G$, we set \begin{equation} \rVec{Z}_V(u):=(1-\delta(u)) \rVec{Z}_V(\ul u) + \delta(u) \rVec{Z}_V(\ol u). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Interpolation of Z_V
nodes.statement: \rVec{Z}_V(u):=(1-\delta(u)) \rVec{Z}_V(\ul u) + \delta(u) \rVec{Z}_V(\ol u).
nodes.label: eq:interpZv

nodes.name: Edge random field Z_E
nodes.statement: We define $\rVec{Z}_E$ as a $p$-variate zero-mean Gaussian random field independent of $\rVec{Z}_V$ whose covariance matrix-valued function is: \begin{equation} \Cov{\rVec{Z}_E(u_1)}{\rVec{Z}_E(u_2)}:=\mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}\Mv{p}{1}{\beta} \in {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}, \end{equation} for $e_i:=e(u_i)$, $\delta_i:={\delta}(u_i)$, $i\in\curly{1,2}$ and where $\beta\in\square{0,1}$ is a fixed parameter.
nodes.statement_short: Z_E is independent of Z_V, independent across edges, with Brownian-bridge covariance on each edge times M_p(1,beta).

nodes.name: Covariance of Z_E
nodes.statement: \Cov{\rVec{Z}_E(u_1)}{\rVec{Z}_E(u_2)}:=\mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}\Mv{p}{1}{\beta} \in {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p},
nodes.label: eq:covZ_E

nodes.name: Validity of the Z_E covariance
nodes.statement: Notice that $\rVec{Z}_E\big|_{e_1}$ is independent from $\rVec{Z}_E\big|_{e_2}$ whenever $e_1 \ne e_2$, in addition $\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}$ is the covariance function of a standard Brownian bridge on $[0,\ell(e_1)]$, whilst $\Mh{p}{1}{\beta}$ is positive semidefinite for $\beta\in[0,1]$. This ensures that (\ref{eq:covZ_E}) is positive semidefinite, as the {element-wise} product of positive semidefinite functions is itself positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: The Z_E covariance is psd: a Brownian-bridge covariance times the psd matrix M_p(1,beta), and Schur products preserve psd.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5 (from definitions)
nodes.statement: The following result comes directly from the above definitions.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation from the definitions of Z_V and Z_E.

nodes.name: Explicit covariances of Z_V and Z_E
nodes.statement: Let ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}$, ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}$ be the covariance mappings associated respectively with the {random fields} $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$. Then, it is true that \begin{equation} {\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)=\Mv{p}{\dVec{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}, \end{equation} for $u_i=(\ul u_i, \ol u_i, \delta_i)\in \mathcal G$ ($i\in\curly{1,2}$), and where $\dVec{\delta}_{{i,V}}$ is the $n$-dimensional vector whose entries are \begin{equation} {\delta}_{{i,{V}}}:=\begin{cases} 1-\delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ul u_i\\ \delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ol u_i\\ 0 \quad &\text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad v\in V. \end{equation} Further, it is true that \begin{equation*} {\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}(u_1,u_2)=\Mv{p}{\mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}. \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}$, ${\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}$ be the covariance mappings associated respectively with the {random fields} $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$.
nodes.statement_short: K_{Z_V} = M_p(delta1' Sigma~ delta2, delta1' X~ delta2) with interpolation weight vectors; K_{Z_E} = Brownian-bridge term times M_p(1,beta).
nodes.label: prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE

nodes.name: Covariance of Z_V at arbitrary points
nodes.statement: {\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)=\Mv{p}{\dVec{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p},

nodes.name: Interpolation weight vector delta_{i,V}
nodes.statement: {\delta}_{{i,{V}}}:=\begin{cases} 1-\delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ul u_i\\ \delta_i \quad &\text{if }v=\ol u_i\\ 0 \quad &\text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad v\in V.
nodes.label: eq:delta_i

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: As a direct implication of Proposition \ref{prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE} in concert with the fact that $\rVec{Z}_V$ and $\rVec{Z}_E$ are independent, we obtain the following.
nodes.statement_short: Add the two covariances of Proposition 5, using independence of Z_V and Z_E.

nodes.name: Covariance of Z
nodes.statement: It is true that \begin{align} &{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)={\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)+{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}(u_1,u_2)\nonumber\\ &=\Mv{p}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}} + \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}} + \beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: K_Z is the sum of the Z_V and Z_E covariances, again of the block form M_p.
nodes.label: cor:explicitExprK_Z

nodes.name: Covariance of Z
nodes.statement: &{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)={\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_V}(u_1,u_2)+{\latMatr{K}}_{\rVec{Z}_E}(u_1,u_2)\nonumber\\ &=\Mv{p}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}\dVec{\delta}_{{2,V}} + \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\dVec \delta_{{1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}}\dVec \delta_{{2,V}} + \beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}.
nodes.label: eq:covZ_full

nodes.name: Matrix-valued metric D as pseudo-variogram of Z
nodes.statement: To do so, we let $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G \times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p \times p}$ be the pseudo-variogram of $\rVec{Z}$, \textit{i.e. } \begin{equation} \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2):=\grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)=\square{\mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(u_1)-Z_j(u_2)}}_{i,j=1}^p. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Distance as pseudo-variogram
nodes.statement: \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2):=\grMatr \Gamma_{\rVec{Z}}(u_1,u_2)=\square{\mathbb{V}ar\round{Z_i(u_1)-Z_j(u_2)}}_{i,j=1}^p.
nodes.label: eq:definitionOfDistance

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6 (sketch)
nodes.statement: A straightforward application of Equation (\ref{eq:pseudoVariogramMatricial}) in concert with tedious calculations provides the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the matrix form of the pseudo-variogram to the covariance of Z and compute.

nodes.name: Explicit form of the multivariate metric
nodes.statement: It is true that \begin{align} \latMatr{D}(u_1,&u_2)=\Mv{p}{\round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}} + \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}-2\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}\nonumber\\ &+\Mv{p}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\mathbbm{1} \round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2} \ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}, \end{align} for $u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal G$, with notation as in Proposition \ref{prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE}.
assumptions: for $u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal G$, with notation as in Proposition \ref{prop:explicit_K_ZV_and_K_ZE}.
nodes.statement_short: D(u1,u2) is the sum of a Z_V block term in Sigma~, X~ and a Z_E block term in edge lengths and positions.
nodes.label: prop:explicitWritingMultivMetric

nodes.name: Explicit multivariate metric
nodes.statement: \latMatr{D}(u_1,&u_2)=\Mv{p}{\round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \round{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}}{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}} + \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}^\top \Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}-2\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {1,V}}^\top \Tilde {\latMatr{X}} \boldsymbol{\delta}_{ {2,V}}}\nonumber\\ &+\Mv{p}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\mathbbm{1} \round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}}{\ell(e_1) \delta_1(1-\delta_1)+\ell(e_2)\delta_2(1-\delta_2) - 2\beta \mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2} \ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}},
nodes.label: eq:explicitWritingMultivMetric

nodes.name: Quasi-metric properties of D
nodes.statement: The matrix-valued expression (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}) satisfies properties similar to the (real-valued) quasi-metrics, \textit{i.e. } it satisfies: \begin{enumerate} \item $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)\geq 0$; \item $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)=0 \iff u_1=u_2$ and $i=j$; \item $\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2) = \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)^\top = \latMatr{D}(u_2,u_1) = \latMatr{D}(u_2,u_1)^\top$ for any $u_1, u_2 \in \mathcal G$; \item The mapping $(u_1,u_2) \mapsto \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_0) \latMatr{A} + \latMatr{A}^\top \latMatr{D}(u_0,u_2) - \latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2) - \latMatr{A}^\top \latMatr{D}(u_0,u_0) \latMatr{A}$ is positive semidefinite for any $u_0 \in \mathcal G$ and any $p\times p$ matrix $\latMatr{A}$ such that $\latMatr{A}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{p}} = {\mathbf{1}_{p}}$; \item {The matrices $\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)-\latMatr{D}(u_0,u_0)$ and $2\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_0)+2\latMatr{D}(u_2,u_0)-\latMatr{D}(u_1,u_2)-3\latMatr{D}(u_0,u_0)$ are symmetric and positive semidefinite for any $u_0,u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal G$.} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: D is nonnegative, vanishes only on the diagonal at coincident points, is symmetric, and satisfies two semidefiniteness inequalities.
nodes.label: prop:actuallyQuasiMetricSpace

nodes.name: Marginals are resistance distances; D is matrix-homogeneous
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges and let $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G\times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}$ as defined in (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}) and having elements $D_{ij}$, $i,j=1,\ldots, p$. Then, the following properties hold: \begin{enumerate} \item for all $i\in\curly{1,\dots,p}$, the distance $D_{ii}$ coincides with the resistance distance defined by \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}, \textit{i.e. } $D_{ii}(u_1,u_2)=d_{R}(u_1,u_2)$; \item the distance $\latMatr{D}$ is matrix-homogeneous, \textit{i.e. } for every $ i\ne j$ and $\,i'\ne j'$, we have $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)=D_{i'j'}(u_1,u_2)$ and $D_{ii}(u_1,u_2)=D_{i'i'}(u_1,u_2)$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges
let $\latMatr{D}: \mathcal G\times \mathcal G \to {[0,+\infty)}^{p\times p}$ as defined in (\ref{eq:definitionOfDistance}) and having elements $D_{ij}$, $i,j=1,\ldots, p$.
nodes.statement_short: Each diagonal entry of D is the resistance metric, and all off-diagonal (and all diagonal) entries coincide.
nodes.label: prop:ourDistProperties

nodes.name: Within-variable distance need not be smaller than cross-variable distance
nodes.statement: Albeit counter-intuitive, the distance within the same variable is not always less than the same distance among variables. In formulae, $D_{ii}(u_1,u_2)\not\leq D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)$, in general.

nodes.name: Asymptotic properties of the metric
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal G}$ be a graph with Euclidean edges and let $\latMatr{Q}$ and ${\latMatr{X}}$ as defined in Equations (\ref{eq:defQ})-(\ref{eq:defXEigen}). Then, the asymptotic results {indicated in Table \ref{tab:asympt}} hold.\par \begin{table} \caption{Asymptotic results with respect to $p$ and $\alpha$. nodes.statement: By the standard properties of the Kronecker product, \begin{align*} &\round{\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}}}\round{\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{C}} + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{D}}} = \\ & = (\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}}) (\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{C}}) + (\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{A}}) \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{D}}} \\ &\quad + \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}}} \round{\latMatr{I}_p \otimes {\latMatr{C}}} + \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{B}}} \round{({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes {\latMatr{D}}} \\ &= (\latMatr{I}_p \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}) + (\latMatr{I}_p({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p))\otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}) \\ &\quad + (({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}) + (({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p)({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p)) \otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}})\\ &= \latMatr{I}_p \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}})+({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}) + (p {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} - 2\cdot {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}+\latMatr{I}_p)\otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}})\\ &=\latMatr{I}_p \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}) + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}})\\ &\quad + \big((p-2)({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) + (p-1) \latMatr{I}_p\big) \otimes ({\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}) \\ &= \latMatr{I}_p \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}} + (p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}) + ({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}-\latMatr{I}_p) \otimes ({\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Throughout this proof, we assume that $\latMatr{L}\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, ${\latMatr{A}}\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_1}$ and ${\latMatr{C}}\in \mathbb{R}^{n_2 \times n_2}$, with $n_1,n_2>0$ and $n=n_1+n_2$.\par \begin{enumerate} \item Assume ${\latMatr{B}}=0$. Then $n-1 = \mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{L}})=\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{A}})+\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{C}})$. But since $\latMatr L {\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0$, it follows that ${\latMatr{A}} \dVec {1}_{n_1}=\dVec 0$ and ${\latMatr{C}} \dVec 1_{n_2}= \dVec0$. This implies that $\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{A}})\leq n_1-1$ and $\mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{C}})\leq n_2 -1$. Contradiction. \item We will show only that ${\latMatr{C}}$ strictly positive definite, as the proof for the other case relies on the same argument. Since $\latMatr C$ is a principal submatrix of $\latMatr L$, it is positive semidefinite. As a consequence, it is sufficient to show that it is invertible. Assume, by contradiction, that ${\latMatr{C}}$ is singular. This is equivalent to assume that $\exists \dVec y\ne \dVec 0$ such that ${\latMatr{C}} \dVec y=\dVec 0$. Since $\latMatr L$ is positive semidefinite we have, for each $\dVec x\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1}$ and for each $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$: \begin{align*} 0 &\leq \begin{bmatrix} \dVec x \\ \gamma \dVec y \end{bmatrix}^\top \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}}\\ {\latMatr{B}}^\top & {\latMatr{C}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dVec x \\ \gamma \dVec y \end{bmatrix}\\ &=\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{A}} \dVec x + \dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} (\gamma \dVec y) + (\gamma \dVec y)^\top {\latMatr{B}}^\top \dVec x + (\gamma \dVec y)^\top {\latMatr{C}} (\gamma \dVec y)=\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{A}} \dVec x + 2 \gamma \dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} \dVec y. \end{align*} If $\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} \dVec y\ne 0$, we can find a suitable $\gamma$ that contradicts the previous inequality. Hence $\dVec x^\top {\latMatr{B}} \dVec y=0$ and therefore, being $\dVec x$ arbitrary, ${\latMatr{B}} \dVec y=\dVec 0$. Consider now the vector $\dVec z:=(0,...,0,\dVec y^\top)^\top$: we have ${\latMatr{L}}\dVec z=\dVec 0$, but clearly $\dVec z$ does not lie in the null space of $\latMatr L$, which is $\curly{\lambda {\mathbf{1}_{n}}\,:\,\lambda\in \mathbb{R}}$. Contradiction. \item Clearly ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}$ is symmetric. Furthermore, the Guttman rank additivity formula \cite[Equation 0.9.2]{zhang_schur_2005} states that $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}})=\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{C}}) + \mathrm{rank}({\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}})$. Here we have $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}})=n-1$ and $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{C}})=n_2$, as a consequence $\mathrm{rank} ({\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}})=n_1-1$. Furthermore, from \citet[Theorem 1.12]{zhang_schur_2005}, being ${\latMatr{C}}$ strictly positive definite and $L$ positive semidefinite, we have that ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}$ is positive semidefinite as well. The last thing that is left to be shown is that the null eigenvector of ${\latMatr{L}}/{\latMatr{C}}$ is ${\dVec 1}_{n_1}$. Since ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$ is the null eigenvector of $\latMatr L$, we get \begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{A}} & {\latMatr{B}} \end{bmatrix}{\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0 \qquad \text{ and }\qquad \begin{bmatrix} {\latMatr{B}}^\top & {\latMatr{C}} \end{bmatrix}{\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0, \end{equation*} videlicet ${\latMatr{A}} \dVec{1}_{n_1}+{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}=\dVec 0$ and ${\latMatr{B}}^\top \dVec{1}_{n_1}+{\latMatr{C}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}=\dVec 0$. Using these relations, the following chain of equivalences concludes the proof: \begin{align*} &({\latMatr{A}}-{\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}^\top) \mathbf{1}_{n_1}= \dVec 0 \iff {\latMatr{A}} \mathbf{1}_{n_1} = {\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1} {\latMatr{B}}^\top \dVec{1}_{n_1}\\ & \iff -{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}={\latMatr{B}} {\latMatr{C}}^{-1}(-{\latMatr{C}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}) \iff -{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2} = -{\latMatr{B}} \dVec{1}_{n_2}. \end{align*} \item Consider the eigendecomposition of $\latMatr L$: \begin{equation} {\latMatr{L}}=\latMatr W \begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \latMatr W^\top, \end{equation} with $\grMatr{\Delta}$ a $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ diagonal matrix with positive diagonal entries. Since $\latMatr W$ is an orthogonal matrix, we have \begin{equation} \begin{split} {\latMatr{L}}^-&=\round{\latMatr W \begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \latMatr W^\top}^-=(\latMatr W^\top)^-\begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^- \latMatr W^-=\latMatr W\begin{bmatrix} \grMatr{\Delta}^{-1} & \dVec 0\\ \dVec 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \latMatr W^\top. \end{split} \end{equation} Therefore ${\latMatr{L}}^-$ is symmetric, is positive semidefinite and with exactly one null eigenvalue, corresponding to the same null-space eigenvector of $\latMatr L$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Rank counting and contradiction for parts 1-2; Guttman rank additivity for Schur complements; eigendecomposition for the pseudo-inverse.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.2
nodes.statement: Recall the eigendecomposition of matrix $\latMatr Q$ given in Equation (\ref{eq:defQEigen}): it is clear that the eigenvalues of $\latMatr Q$ are the elements on the diagonal of the matrix \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2}\round{\grMatr{\Lambda}^-+\sqrt{(\grMatr{\Lambda}^{-})^2-2\alpha(p-2)\grMatr{\Lambda}^-+\alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n}+\alpha(p-2)\latMatr{I}_n}, \end{equation*} which are $\curly{f(\lambda^-)\;:\;\lambda\in \curly{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n}}$, where {$\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ are the diagonal entries of $\grMatr{\Lambda}$ (positive, except for $\lambda_n$ that is null) and} \begin{equation*} f(\lambda^-):=\frac{1}{2}\round{\lambda^-+\sqrt{\round{\lambda^-}^2-2\alpha(p-2)\lambda^-+\alpha^2 p^2}+\alpha(p-2)}. \end{equation*} Here, we recall that, for a scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda^-:=\lambda^{-1}$ if $\lambda \ne 0$ and $\lambda^-:=0$ if $\lambda=0$. It is straightforward to show that $\lambda^- \mapsto f(\lambda^-)$ is a strictly increasing function on $\lambda^- \geq 0$. As a consequence, since $\lambda \mapsto \lambda^-$ is strictly decreasing on $\lambda > 0$, $\lambda \mapsto f(\lambda^-)$ is strictly decreasing on $\lambda>0$. Therefore, $\lambda_1\geq\dots\geq \lambda_{n-1}$ are mapped in $\lambda_1(\latMatr Q)=f(\lambda_1^{-1})\leq\dots\leq \lambda_{n-1}(\latMatr Q)= f(\lambda_{n-1}^{-1})$. For the case $\lambda_n=0$, we have $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)=f(\lambda_n^-)=f(0)=\frac{1}{2}\round{\alpha p + \alpha(p-2)}=\alpha(p-1)$. In addition, since $\lambda_n=0<\lambda_1(\latMatr Q)$, we have $\alpha(p-1) = \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) < \lambda_1(\latMatr Q)$. \\ Finally, to show that $\latMatr Q {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \alpha(p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, it is sufficient to notice from the eigendecomposition of $\latMatr Q$ given in Equation (\ref{eq:defQEigen}) that ${\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, being (proportional to) the last column of $\latMatr W$, is an eigenvector of $\latMatr Q$. And by the above result it is clear that the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda_n(\latMatr Q)=\alpha(p-1)$. This concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Useful identities for Sigma, L, Q, X
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr L$ be an $n \times n$ quasi-Laplacian matrix, ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}={\latMatr{L}}^-$ and $\alpha >0$. Furthermore, let $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr X$ as defined in Subsection \ref{ssec:constructionZ_V}. Then the following holds: \begin{enumerate} \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}$, $\latMatr L$, $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr X$ commute; \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= {\latMatr{L}}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} = \latMatr{I}_n-\frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$; \item $\latMatr Q^2-\alpha^2 (p-1) \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr Q {\latMatr{L}}- \alpha (p-2) \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}= \matr 0$; \item ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2 (p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q - \alpha (p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n + \frac{\alpha}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}=\matr 0$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.3
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item It is sufficient to notice that all the matrices share the same eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$, \textit{i.e. } for any ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}\in\curly{{\grMatr{\Sigma}},\latMatr L,\latMatr Q,\latMatr X}$, there are two diagonal matrices $\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}},\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}}$ such that ${\latMatr{A}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}}\matr W^\top$ and ${\latMatr{B}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top$. Therefore \begin{align*} {\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{B}}&=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top\\ &=\latMatr W\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top = {\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{A}}. \end{align*} \item By exploiting the diagonalisations ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \latMatr W^\top$ (Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}) and ${\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}^- \latMatr W^\top$ (Eqs. (\ref{eq:eigL1}) and (\ref{eq:eigL2})), we get: \begin{align*} {\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \grMatr{\Lambda}^- \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W (\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n) \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top. \end{align*} Given that $\latMatr L$ is a quasi-Laplacian matrix, its eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$ can be written as \begin{equation*} \latMatr W = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix}, \end{equation*} where $\latMatr U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (n-1)}$ and $n c^2=1$. Therefore \begin{align} \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \matr 0_{(n-1)\times(n-1)} & \matr 0_{(n-1)\times 1}\\ \matr 0_{1 \times (n-1)} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U^\top \\ c {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top \end{bmatrix}= \frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top, \end{align} and this concludes the proof. \item From the definition (\ref{eq:defQ}) of $\latMatr Q$, one has: \begin{equation*} 2\latMatr Q - {\latMatr{L}}- \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n = \sqrt{{\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n}. \end{equation*} Now, taking the square of both sides (recall that $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr L$ commute): \begin{align*} &4 \latMatr Q^2 + {\latMatr{L}}^2 + \alpha^2 (p-2)^2 \latMatr{I}_n - 4 \latMatr Q{\latMatr{L}}- 4 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr Q + 2 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr L\\ &= {\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n. \end{align*} By grouping the common terms and dividing everything by $4$ we get the desired result. \item To show the second assertion, it is sufficient to multiply the first equation by ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} = {\latMatr{L}}^-$: \begin{align*} &{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2(p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q ({\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}) - \alpha(p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) ({\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}) = \matr 0\\ &{\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q^2 - \alpha^2 (p-1) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \latMatr Q + \frac{1}{n} \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha (p-2) {\grMatr{\Sigma}} \latMatr Q + \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n \\ &\quad - \frac{\alpha (p-2)}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}=\matr 0, \end{align*} where we have used ${\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ and $\latMatr Q {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \lambda_n(\latMatr Q) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}= \alpha(p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$ (Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Common eigenvectors give commutation; spectral computation of Sigma L; square the defining equation of Q.

nodes.name: Commutation via shared eigenvectors
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to notice that all the matrices share the same eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$, \textit{i.e. } for any ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}\in\curly{{\grMatr{\Sigma}},\latMatr L,\latMatr Q,\latMatr X}$, there are two diagonal matrices $\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}},\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}}$ such that ${\latMatr{A}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}}\matr W^\top$ and ${\latMatr{B}}=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top$. Therefore \begin{align*} {\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{B}}&=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top=\latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top\\ &=\latMatr W\grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{B}} \latMatr W^\top \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda}_{\latMatr{A}} \latMatr W^\top = {\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{A}}. \end{align*}

(\ref{eq:eigL1}) and (\ref{eq:eigL2})), we get: \begin{align*} {\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr{L}}= \latMatr W \grMatr{\Lambda} \grMatr{\Lambda}^- \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr W (\latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr{J}_n) \latMatr W^\top = \latMatr{I}_n - \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top. \end{align*} Given that $\latMatr L$ is a quasi-Laplacian matrix, its eigenvector matrix $\latMatr W$ can be written as \begin{equation*} \latMatr W = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix}, \end{equation*} where $\latMatr U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (n-1)}$ and $n c^2=1$. Therefore \begin{align} \latMatr W \latMatr{J}_n \latMatr W^\top = \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U & c {\mathbf{1}_{n}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \matr 0_{(n-1)\times(n-1)} & \matr 0_{(n-1)\times 1}\\ \matr 0_{1 \times (n-1)} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr U^\top \\ c {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top \end{bmatrix}= \frac{1}{n} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} {\mathbf{1}_{n}}^\top, \end{align} and this concludes the proof.

nodes.statement: From the definition (\ref{eq:defQ}) of $\latMatr Q$, one has: \begin{equation*} 2\latMatr Q - {\latMatr{L}}- \alpha (p-2) \latMatr{I}_n = \sqrt{{\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n}. \end{equation*} Now, taking the square of both sides (recall that $\latMatr Q$ and $\latMatr L$ commute): \begin{align*} &4 \latMatr Q^2 + {\latMatr{L}}^2 + \alpha^2 (p-2)^2 \latMatr{I}_n - 4 \latMatr Q{\latMatr{L}}- 4 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr Q + 2 \alpha (p-2) \latMatr L\\ &= {\latMatr{L}}^2 - 2\alpha (p-2) {\latMatr{L}}+ \alpha^2 p^2 \latMatr{I}_n. \end{align*} By grouping the common terms and dividing everything by $4$ we get the desired result.

nodes.name: Sum of matrices with complementary eigenvalue bounds
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr X,\latMatr Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric matrices. For $i\in\curly{1,\dots,n}$, let $\lambda_i(\latMatr X)$ and $\lambda_i(\latMatr Y)$ denote the $i^\text{th}$ eigenvalues of $\latMatr X$ and $\latMatr Y$, respectively. Let $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\lambda_i(\latMatr X)\geq c$ and $\lambda_i(\latMatr Y)\geq -c$ for all $i\in\curly{1,\dots,n}$. Then $\latMatr X+\latMatr Y$ is positive semidefinite.
assumptions: Let $\latMatr X,\latMatr Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric matrices.
Let $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\lambda_i(\latMatr X)\geq c$ and $\lambda_i(\latMatr Y)\geq -c$ for all $i\in\curly{1,\dots,n}$.
conclusions: Then $\latMatr X+\latMatr Y$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr X=\latMatr W_1\grMatr{\Delta}_1 \latMatr W_1^\top$ and $\latMatr Y=\latMatr W_2\grMatr{\Delta}_2 \latMatr W_2^\top$ be the eigendecompositions of $\latMatr X$ and $\latMatr Y$ and let $\dVec v\in\mathbb{R}^n$. In the following lines, we have defined $\dVec a:=\latMatr W_1^\top \dVec v$ and $\dVec b:= \latMatr W_2^\top \dVec v$. \begin{align*} \dVec v^\top (\latMatr X+\latMatr Y) \dVec v&=\dVec v^\top \latMatr W_1 \Delta_1 \latMatr W_1^\top \dVec v +\dVec v \latMatr W_2 \grMatr{\Delta}_2 \latMatr W_2^\top\dVec v= \dVec a^\top \grMatr{\Delta}_1\dVec a +\dVec b^\top \grMatr{\Delta}_2\dVec b \\ & = \sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(\latMatr X) a_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i(\latMatr Y) b_i^2\geq c \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - c \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\\ &=c(\dVec a^\top \dVec a - \dVec b^\top \dVec b) = c(\dVec v^\top \dVec v-\dVec v^\top \dVec v)=0. \end{align*} Videlicet, $\latMatr X+\latMatr Y$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: Write the quadratic form in the two eigenbases and bound by c|v|^2 - c|v|^2 = 0.

nodes.name: K-tilde is the Moore-Penrose inverse of Theta
nodes.statement: Let $\latMatr{L}$ an $n\times n$ Laplacian matrix, let ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}:={\latMatr{L}}^-$ its Moore-Penrose inverse and let $\alpha > 0$. Let $\grMatr{\Theta}$, $\latMatr Q$, $\latMatr X$, $k_1$, $k_2$, $\Tilde{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}$ and $\Tilde{\latMatr X}$ as described in Subsection \ref{ssec:constructionZ_V}. Finally let: \begin{equation} \Tilde {\latMatr K} := \Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde {\latMatr X}}. \end{equation} Then $\Tilde{\latMatr K}=\grMatr{\Theta}^-$.
assumptions: Let $\latMatr{L}$ an $n\times n$ Laplacian matrix, let ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}:={\latMatr{L}}^-$ its Moore-Penrose inverse and let $\alpha > 0$.
nodes.label: lem:KinverseTheta

nodes.name: Definition of K-tilde
nodes.statement: \Tilde {\latMatr K} := \Mv{p}{\Tilde {\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde {\latMatr X}}.
nodes.label: eq:defKTilde

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.5
nodes.statement: In order to show that $\Tilde{\latMatr K} = \grMatr{\Theta}^-$, by definition of the Moore-Penrose inverse, we need to prove \begin{enumerate} \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}$ and $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}$ are symmetric, \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \grMatr{\Theta}$, \item $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}$. \end{enumerate} To show symmetry, recall from Lemma \ref{lem:usefulIdentities} that all the matrices $\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ commute. As a consequence, $\forall {\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}},{\latMatr{C}},{\latMatr{D}} \in \curly{\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}$, it holds (Lemma \ref{lem:MpMp_expr}): \begin{align*} &\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}} = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{A}}+(p-1){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}{{\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{A}}+{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{B}}+(p-2){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}. \end{align*} In addition, $\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}^\top=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}^\top}{{\latMatr{B}}^\top}=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}$, as ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}$ are symmetric. Therefore, \begin{align*} &\round{\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}}^\top = \Tilde{\latMatr K}^\top \grMatr{\Theta}^\top = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}^\top \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}^\top \\ &= \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}^\top + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}^\top}{\latMatr X^\top + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}^\top} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}^\top}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &=\Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} + \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} + \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} + k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\latMatr X + k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}. \end{align*} The same arguments show that $\round{\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}}^\top = \Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}$. To prove the other two relations, we start with following equalities. In the next lines, we used Lemmas \ref{lem:MpMp_expr}, \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ} and \ref{lem:usefulIdentities}. \begin{align*} \allowdisplaybreaks &\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} - \alpha(p-1)\latMatr X}{{\latMatr Q}\latMatr X-\alpha {\grMatr{\Sigma}}-\alpha(p-2)\latMatr X}\\ &\quad=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\alpha(p-1)\frac{1}{-\alpha(p-1)}(\latMatr{I}_n-{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr Q})}{\frac{1}{-\alpha(p-1)}({\latMatr Q}-{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\latMatr Q}^2)-\alpha{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\alpha(p-2)\latMatr X}=\Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\alpha (p-1)\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n - \frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha(p-2)\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad =\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta}\, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Mv{p}{k_1 {\latMatr Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-\alpha (p-1) k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\latMatr Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha k_2 (p-2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad=\Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\grMatr{\Theta}\, \Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \grMatr{\Theta} = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha (k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} \\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{-\alpha(p-1)(k_2-k_1){\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha^2 (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{\alpha^2(p-1)(k_2-k_1){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} - \alpha(k_1-k_2){\latMatr Q}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} +\alpha^2(p-2)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{\alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ \intertext{As a consequence:} &\grMatr{\Theta}\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \grMatr{\Theta} \round{\latMatr K+\Mv{p}{k_1 {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{k_2{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}} \grMatr{\Theta}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} + \Mv{p}{\alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}\\ &\quad = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}+\frac{\alpha}{n}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \alpha^2 p (p-1)(k_1-k_2){\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n -\frac{\alpha}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}-\alpha^2 p (k_1-k_2) {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n} = \grMatr{\Theta}. \intertext{Similarly we prove that $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}$:} &\latMatr{K}\grMatr{\Theta} \latMatr{K} = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\latMatr X} \Mv{p}{\latMatr{I}_n}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}} = \Mv{p}{{\grMatr{\Sigma}} -\frac{1}{n} \latMatr X {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}{-\frac{1}{n(p-1)}{\grMatr{\Sigma}} {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}} + \latMatr X - nodes.name: Reduce to the Moore-Penrose conditions
nodes.statement: In order to show that $\Tilde{\latMatr K} = \grMatr{\Theta}^-$, by definition of the Moore-Penrose inverse, we need to prove \begin{enumerate} \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K}$ and $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta}$ are symmetric, \item $\grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} = \grMatr{\Theta}$, \item $\Tilde{\latMatr K} \grMatr{\Theta} \Tilde{\latMatr K} = \Tilde{\latMatr K}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: M_p blocks with commuting entries commute
nodes.statement: To show symmetry, recall from Lemma \ref{lem:usefulIdentities} that all the matrices $\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}$ commute. As a consequence, $\forall {\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}},{\latMatr{C}},{\latMatr{D}} \in \curly{\latMatr Q,\alpha \latMatr{I}_n, {\grMatr{\Sigma}}, \latMatr X, {\mathbf{1}_{n\times n}}}$, it holds (Lemma \ref{lem:MpMp_expr}): \begin{align*} &\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}} = \Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-1){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}{{\latMatr{A}}{\latMatr{D}}+{\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{C}}+(p-2){\latMatr{B}}{\latMatr{D}}}\\ &=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{A}}+(p-1){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}{{\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{A}}+{\latMatr{C}}{\latMatr{B}}+(p-2){\latMatr{D}}{\latMatr{B}}}=\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{C}}}{{\latMatr{D}}}\Mv{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}. \end{align*}

nodes.statement: In addition, $\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}^\top=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}^\top}{{\latMatr{B}}^\top}=\Mh{p}{{\latMatr{A}}}{{\latMatr{B}}}$, as ${\latMatr{A}},{\latMatr{B}}$ are symmetric. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: We first show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is quasi-Laplacian. To this end, we need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric, positive semidefinite, $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np}=\dVec 0$, and $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has only one null eigenvalue. \begin{enumerate} \item Since $\latMatr{Q}$ and $\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ are symmetric and $\grMatr{\Theta}:=\Mh{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}$, $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric. \item First recall that $\grMatr{\Theta} = \matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) + {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$: we aim to apply Lemma \ref{lem:sumOfMatricesPD} to the matrix $\grMatr{\Theta}$ with $\latMatr X:=\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$ and $\latMatr Y:={\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$. In the following, we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})$ to denote the vector of eigenvalues of ${\latMatr{A}}$. In addition, the inequalities apply to all elements: we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$ as a shortcut of $\forall i\in\curly{1,\dots,n},\,\lambda_i({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$, for an $n\times n$ matrix ${\latMatr{A}}$. \begin{align*} \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{X}) &= \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) ={\mathbf{1}_{p}} \otimes (\dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}) + \alpha) \\ &\geq \lambda_n(\latMatr{Q}) +\alpha = \alpha (p-1) +\alpha = \alpha p\\ \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Y}) &= \dVec{\lambda}({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} \otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \begin{bmatrix} p\\ 0\\ \vdots\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\otimes \begin{bmatrix} -\alpha \\ \vdots \\ -\alpha \end{bmatrix}\geq -\alpha p. \end{align*} Therefore $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is positive semidefinite. \item To show $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np} = \dVec 0$, given the special structure of $\grMatr{\Theta}$, it is sufficient to show that \begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{1}_{np} = \dVec 0, \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. } $\latMatr{Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \alpha (p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, {which has already been proved in Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}}. \item We now need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has no other null eigenvalues, \textit{i.e. } the only solution to \begin{equation} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \latMatr{Q} & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & \latMatr{Q} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dVec v_1\\ \dVec v_2\\ \vdots\\ \dVec v_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dVec 0 \\ \dVec 0 \\ \vdots\\ \dVec 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{equation} is (up to a multiplicative constant) $\dVec v_1=\dots=\dVec v_n={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$. By reading Equation (\ref{eq:Theta_v_equal_0}) by blocks, we get the following: $\forall i \in \curly{1,\dots,n}$ \begin{align*} \latMatr{Q} \dVec v_i - \alpha \sum_{k\ne i} \dVec v_k = \dVec 0. \end{align*} Taking now the difference for $i=i$ and $i=j$, we get \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)(\dVec v_i-\dVec v_j)=\dVec 0 \end{equation*} and, since $\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ is strictly positive definite directly by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, we obtain that $\dVec v_i=\dVec v_j=:\dVec v$ for all $i,j$. The problem thus becomes \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1)\latMatr{I}_n) \dVec v = \dVec 0. \end{equation*} To conclude it is sufficient to notice that the eigenvalues of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1) \latMatr{I}_n$ are $\lambda_i(\latMatr{Q}) - \alpha (p-1)$ and, by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, all the eigenvalues are not less than $\alpha(p-1)$ and exactly one achieve such a value. As a consequence, the kernel of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n$ has dimension one and, since we already know that $(\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n){\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0$, the only possibility is $\dVec v={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$. \end{enumerate} That $\grMatr{\Theta}^-$ is also a quasi-Laplacian matrix comes from Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and the closure of the set of quasi-Laplacian matrices under Moore-Penrose inversion (Proposition \ref{prop:quasiLaplacianProperties}).

nodes.name: List the quasi-Laplacian properties to check
nodes.statement: We first show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is quasi-Laplacian. To this end, we need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric, positive semidefinite, $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np}=\dVec 0$, and $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has only one null eigenvalue.
nodes.statement_short: List the quasi-Laplacian properties to check

nodes.name: Symmetry
nodes.statement: Since $\latMatr{Q}$ and $\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ are symmetric and $\grMatr{\Theta}:=\Mh{p}{\latMatr{Q}}{-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n}$, $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry

nodes.name: Positive semidefinite via Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: First recall that $\grMatr{\Theta} = \matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) + {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$: we aim to apply Lemma \ref{lem:sumOfMatricesPD} to the matrix $\grMatr{\Theta}$ with $\latMatr X:=\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$ and $\latMatr Y:={\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}\otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)$. In the following, we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})$ to denote the vector of eigenvalues of ${\latMatr{A}}$. In addition, the inequalities apply to all elements: we write $\dVec{\lambda}({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$ as a shortcut of $\forall i\in\curly{1,\dots,n},\,\lambda_i({\latMatr{A}})\geq c$, for an $n\times n$ matrix ${\latMatr{A}}$. \begin{align*} \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{X}) &= \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p \otimes (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \dVec{\lambda}(\matr{\latMatr{I}}_p) \otimes \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n) ={\mathbf{1}_{p}} \otimes (\dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Q}) + \alpha) \\ &\geq \lambda_n(\latMatr{Q}) +\alpha = \alpha (p-1) +\alpha = \alpha p\\ \dVec{\lambda}(\latMatr{Y}) &= \dVec{\lambda}({\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}} \otimes (-\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)) = \begin{bmatrix} p\\ 0\\ \vdots\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\otimes \begin{bmatrix} -\alpha \\ \vdots \\ -\alpha \end{bmatrix}\geq -\alpha p. \end{align*} Therefore $\grMatr{\Theta}$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: Positive semidefinite via Lemma A.4

nodes.name: Theta 1 = 0 via Q 1 = alpha(p-1) 1
nodes.statement: To show $\grMatr{\Theta} \dVec{1}_{np} = \dVec 0$, given the special structure of $\grMatr{\Theta}$, it is sufficient to show that \begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{1}_{np} = \dVec 0, \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. } $\latMatr{Q} {\mathbf{1}_{n}} = \alpha (p-1) {\mathbf{1}_{n}}$, {which has already been proved in Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}}.
nodes.statement_short: Theta 1 = 0 via Q 1 = alpha(p-1) 1

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the null eigenvector
nodes.statement: We now need to show that $\grMatr{\Theta}$ has no other null eigenvalues, \textit{i.e. } the only solution to \begin{equation} \begin{bmatrix} \latMatr{Q} & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \latMatr{Q} & \dots & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & -\alpha \latMatr{I}_n & \dots & \latMatr{Q} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dVec v_1\\ \dVec v_2\\ \vdots\\ \dVec v_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dVec 0 \\ \dVec 0 \\ \vdots\\ \dVec 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{equation} is (up to a multiplicative constant) $\dVec v_1=\dots=\dVec v_n={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$. By reading Equation (\ref{eq:Theta_v_equal_0}) by blocks, we get the following: $\forall i \in \curly{1,\dots,n}$ \begin{align*} \latMatr{Q} \dVec v_i - \alpha \sum_{k\ne i} \dVec v_k = \dVec 0. \end{align*} Taking now the difference for $i=i$ and $i=j$, we get \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n)(\dVec v_i-\dVec v_j)=\dVec 0 \end{equation*} and, since $\latMatr{Q}+\alpha \latMatr{I}_n$ is strictly positive definite directly by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, we obtain that $\dVec v_i=\dVec v_j=:\dVec v$ for all $i,j$. The problem thus becomes \begin{equation*} (\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1)\latMatr{I}_n) \dVec v = \dVec 0. \end{equation*} To conclude it is sufficient to notice that the eigenvalues of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha(p-1) \latMatr{I}_n$ are $\lambda_i(\latMatr{Q}) - \alpha (p-1)$ and, by Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvaluesQ}, all the eigenvalues are not less than $\alpha(p-1)$ and exactly one achieve such a value. As a consequence, the kernel of $\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n$ has dimension one and, since we already know that $(\latMatr{Q}-\alpha (p-1)\latMatr{I}_n){\mathbf{1}_{n}}=\dVec 0$, the only possibility is $\dVec v={\mathbf{1}_{n}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of the null eigenvector

nodes.statement: It is sufficient to apply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalentFormPositDef} with $X:=V$. We show that the $np\times np$ matrix $[\latMatr K(v_i,v_j)]_{i,j=1}^{np}$ is positive semidefinite. First, notice that $[\latMatr K(v_i,v_j)]_{i,j=1}^{np}=\Mh{p}{\Tilde{\grMatr{\Sigma}}}{\Tilde{\latMatr X}}=\Tilde{\latMatr K}$. Since $\Tilde{\latMatr K}\in \mathbb{R}^{np \times np}$ is positive semidefinite (see Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}), each matrix ${\latMatr{C}}$ as defined in Proposition \ref{prop:equivalentFormPositDef}, being a principal submatrix of $\matr {\Tilde{\latMatr K}}$, is positive semidefinite as well. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The proof of this point is straightforward, as the pseudo variogram only takes non-negative values. \item {The condition $u_1 = u_2$ and $i=j$ is sufficient to have $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2)=0$ due to the fact that the diagonal entries of $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_1,u_1)$ are zero. Let us show that it is also necessary. From the definition of the pseudo-variogram as per Equation (\ref{eq:pseudoVariogramDef}), $D_{ij}(u_1,u_2) = 0$ if and only if $Z_i(u_1) = Z_j(u_2)$. Given the correlation structure (\ref{eq:covZ_V_onV}) at the vertices, the variance-covariance matrix $\Tilde{\latMatr{K}}$ of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ is quasi-Laplacian (Lemma \ref{lem:KinverseTheta} and Proposition \ref{prop:ThetaQuasiLaplacian}) and thus it has only one null eigenvalue associated with the vector ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}$. That is, the only non-trivial linear combination of $\rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$ having a zero variance is, up to a constant factor, ${\mathbf{1}_{np}}^\top \rVec{Z}_V\big|_V$. Therefore, $Z_{V,i}(u_1) = Z_{V,j}(u_2)$ for $u_1, u_2 \in V$ only if $i=j$ and $u_1=u_2$. Given the linear interpolation on the edges (Equation (\ref{eq:interpZv})), the same holds true for any two points $u_1$ and $u_2$ belonging to $\mathcal G$. \item The claim stems from Equations (\ref{sympseudo}) and (\ref{eq:explicitWritingMultivMetric}). \item Let $u_0,u_1,\ldots,u_n \in \mathcal{G}$ and $\dVec{c}_1,\dots, \dVec{c}_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$. Let $\dVec{c}_0=-\latMatr{A}\sum_{i=1}^n \dVec{c}_i$, where $\latMatr{A}$ is a $p \times p$ matrix such that $\latMatr{A}^\top {\mathbf{1}_{p}} = {\mathbf{1}_{p}}$. Then, from Equation (\ref{eq:negativesemidef}), one has: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \sum_{i,j=0}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_j) \dVec{c}_j \\ &= \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_j) \dVec{c}_j + \sum_{i=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_i,u_0) \dVec{c}_0 + \sum_{j=1}^n \dVec{c}_0^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\rVec{Z}}}(u_0,u_j) \dVec{c}_j + \dVec{c}_0^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0) \dVec{c}_0\\ &= \sum_{i,j=1}^n \dVec{c}_i^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_j)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_0)\latMatr{A}-\latMatr{A}^\top \grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_j)+\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\latMatr{A}\right] \dVec{c}_j, \end{split} \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. }, the mapping $(u,v) \mapsto -[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u,v)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u,u_0)\latMatr{A}-\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,v)+\latMatr{A}^\top\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\latMatr{A}]$ is positive semidefinite (Equation \ref{eq:positiveSemidef}). \item Taking $\dVec{c}_1 = \ldots = \dVec{c}_n := \dVec{c}$ and $\latMatr{A} {=\latMatr{I}_p}$, one gets \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \sum_{i,j=1}^n \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_j)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_i,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_j)+\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)\right] \dVec{c}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Accounting for the fact that $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}^\top$ and $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_1)=\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_2)$, one obtains, for $n=1$ and $u_0=u_2$: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)\right] \dVec{c}, \end{split} \end{equation*} and for $n=2$: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} 0 &\geq \dVec{c}^\top \left[\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)+3\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)-2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_0)-2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_0)\right] \dVec{c}, \end{split} \end{equation*} \textit{i.e. }, $\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)$ and $2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_0)+2\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_2,u_0)-\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_1,u_2)-3\grMatr{\Gamma}_{{\bm{Z}}}(u_0,u_0)$ are positive semidefinite matrices. } \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Split into vertex and edge contributions
nodes.statement: We split the computation of the distances (the one proposed here, ${\latMatr{D}}$, and the one defined by \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}, $d_{R}$) in two: the contribution (\textit{i.e. } the variogram) of the $\rVec{Z}_V$ process and the one of $\rVec{Z}_E$, denoted via the superscripts $V$ and $E$ respectively.

nodes.name: Edge contributions match
nodes.statement: We show that ${\latMatr{D}}_{ii}^V(u_1,u_2)=d_{R}^V(u_1,u_2)$ and ${\latMatr{D}}_{ii}^E(u_1,u_2)=d_{R}^E(u_1,u_2)$. The latter comes straightforwardly by comparing the diagonal entries of Equation (\ref{eq:covZ_E}), \textit{i.e. } $\mathbbm{1}\round{e_1=e_2}\ell(e_1)\round{\delta_1 \wedge \delta_2 - \delta_1 \delta_2}$, with the kernel $R_e$ in \citet[Equation 15]{anderes_isotropic_2020}.
nodes.statement_short: Edge contributions match

nodes.name: Vertex contribution equals delta' Sigma delta
nodes.statement: Thus, let us show that ${\latMatr{D}}_{ii}^V(u_1,u_2)=d_{R}^V(u_1,u_2)$. Let $u_1,u_2\in \mathcal G$ {and $k_{V,ii}$ be the $i$-th diagonal entry of {$\latMatr K_{\rVec{Z}_V}$}. nodes.name: Recall the Anderes et al. covariance Sigma_A
nodes.statement: It is left to show that this quantity coincides with the resistance counterpart of \cite{anderes_isotropic_2020}. They define their covariance matrix, here denoted by ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}_{\latMatr{A}}$, as the (proper) inverse of a modified Laplacian matrix $\latMatr{L}$, where a one has been added on an arbitrary diagonal entry. In formulae: ${\grMatr{\Sigma}}_{\latMatr{A}}:=({\latMatr{L}}+\dVec e_j \dVec e_j^\top)^{-1}$, where $\dVec e_j$ is the $j^\text{th}$ vector of the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$. It follows directly from \citet[Equation 13]{anderes_isotropic_2020} that $d_{R}^V=\round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}^\top {\grMatr{\Sigma}}_{\latMatr{A}} \round{\dVec{\delta}_{1,V}-\dVec{\delta}_{2,V}}$.\par

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement: We start with the case $p=1$ and observe that, by Bochner's theorem \citep{bochner1955harmonic}, a continuous mapping $C: \mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}} \to \mathbb{R}$ is positive semidefinite if and only if $$ C(\dVec{x}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}}} \exp(\mathsf{i} \dVec{x}^{\top} \dVec{\omega}) G({\rm d}\dVec{\omega}), \qquad \dVec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}}, $$ for $G$ being a non-decreasing and bounded measure in $\mathbb{R}^m$. Here, $\mathsf{i}$ denotes the unit complex number. Using the above representation, \cite{cambanis1983symmetric} show that a mapping $K: [0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ belongs to the class $\Phi_m^1$ if and only if Equation (\ref{eq:alpha-1}) holds for $p= 1$ and for $F$ being non-decreasing and bounded. {In particular, choosing a Dirac measure for $F$, one finds that $t \mapsto \omega_{m^\prime}(rt)$ belongs to $\Phi_m^1$ for any $r \geq 0$, that is, $\omega_{m^\prime}(r d_M(\cdot,\cdot))$ is positive semidefinite on $\mathbb{R}^{m^\prime}$.}\par We now address the general case with $p \geq 1$. First, consider a matrix-valued mapping $\latMatr{K}$ belonging to the class $\Phi_m^p$. We invoke the extension of Bochner's theorem to the $p$-variate case \citep{cramer1940theory}, for which a continuous mapping $\latMatr{C}: \mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}} \to \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ is positive semidefinite if and only if $$ \latMatr{C}(\dVec{x}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}}} \exp(\mathsf{i} \dVec{x}^{\top} \dVec{\omega}) \latMatr{G}({\rm d}\dVec{\omega}), \qquad \dVec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}}, $$ for $\latMatr{G}$ a bounded {complex Hermitian} matrix-valued measure. Hence, the same calculations as much as in \cite{cambanis1983symmetric} show that the representation (\ref{eq:alpha-1}) holds for a bounded {symmetric} real matrix-valued measure $\latMatr{F}$ {(that $\latMatr{F}$ is bounded stems from the fact that $\latMatr{K}(0)$ is finite)}. To finish this part of the proof we need to show that ${\rm d}\latMatr{F}(r)$ is positive semidefinite for any $r \geq 0$, which happens if and only if the mapping $$ H_{{\dVec{c}}}(r) := \dVec{c}^\top {\latMatr{F}}({\rm d}r) \dVec{c}, \quad r \in [0,+\infty),$$ is non-negative for any arbitrary $\dVec{c} \in \mathbb{R}^p$. To this end, consider a $p$-variate random field $\rVec{Z}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{{m^\prime}}$ with isotropic covariance $\latMatr{K}$, and define $Z_{\dVec{c}} := \dVec{c}^\top \dVec{Z}$, which is a univariate random field with isotropic covariance $K_{\dVec{c}} = \dVec{c}^\top \latMatr{K} \dVec{c}$. Hence, $K_{\dVec{c}}$ obeys to the representation provided by \cite{cambanis1983symmetric}, with a measure $F_{\dVec{c}}$ such that $$ {F_{\dVec{c}} = \dVec{c}^\top \latMatr{F} \dVec{c}}. $$ This proves the sufficiency part of the theorem by noting that $F_{\dVec{c}}$ is non-decreasing. \par {Reciprocally, assume that the representation (\ref{eq:alpha-1}) holds with a bounded symmetric matrix-valued measure $\latMatr{F}$ such that ${\rm d}\latMatr{F}(r)$ is positive semidefinite for any $r \geq 0$. Being positive semidefinite on $\mathbb{R}^{m^\prime}$ for any $r \geq 0$, $\omega_{m^\prime}(r d_M(\cdot,\cdot))$ is the covariance function of a univariate Gaussian random field $Z_r$ on $\mathbb{R}^{m^\prime}$. Accordingly, the matrix-valued mapping $\omega_{m^\prime}(r d_M(\cdot,\cdot)) {\mathbf{1}_{p\times p}}$ belongs to $\Phi_m^p$ as the covariance function of $Z_r {\mathbf{1}_{p}}$, and so do the mappings $\omega_{m^\prime}(r d_M(\cdot,\cdot)) {\rm d}\latMatr{F}(r)$ and $\latMatr{K}(d_M(\cdot,\cdot))$ owing to the fact that the set of positive semidefinite functions is closed under sums, element-wise products, and pointwise limits.}
nodes.statement_short: Scalar case via Bochner and Cambanis et al.; matrix case via Cramer's theorem and projections c'K c for necessity, closure properties for sufficiency.
